entries.title: Begin with your voice
entries.summary: Use your baby’s name and tell them what is happening. Pause so a sound or gesture can become part of the conversation.
entries.cue: You are holding or caring for your baby, with a moment to talk and listen.
detail: A bath about to begin, the part of the body being washed, or the room you are entering can give you something to talk about. Use the words you know and speak gently.

Let your baby see your face. After saying something, wait and notice their response. You might echo a sound or answer a gesture, then leave another pause. The book treats these early exchanges as conversation.
If your baby has an older sibling, another conversation can begin while that child plays: with the baby awake, talk about what their sibling is doing.

entries.title: Read a little of your book aloud
entries.summary: In the first few months, a book you want to read can become something to share: read it aloud with your baby nearby.
entries.cue: You have something you would enjoy reading and your baby is awake and comfortable.
detail: Davies and Uzodike describe early reading as a chance to hear the sounds and rhythm of language. The book does not have to be a baby book; you can read from one that interests you.
Simple picture books are another option. If a picture catches your baby’s attention, you can describe it or stay with that page.

entries.title: Watch a hand’s shadow
entries.summary: Hold your hand with light behind it and let its shadow offer something for your baby to notice.
entries.cue: Your baby is awake, comfortable and interested in looking.
detail: The authors include hand shadows among the simple things a young baby can watch. Notice where their gaze settles and give them time to look.

They also describe light and shadow moving through leaves and branches, or a high-contrast picture within the baby’s view. Follow the interest you see; looking away or becoming upset is a reason to stop or change what is offered.

entries.title: A mobile for quiet looking
entries.summary: The authors describe light, slowly moving mobiles for an awake baby to watch. Their visual mobiles are fragile and meant for looking; reaching and batting call for a different kind of material.
entries.cue: Your baby is interested in watching a slow movement or a changing view.
detail: The book’s examples include black-and-white shapes, reflective colored octahedrons, shades of one color, and paper figures that seem to dance. The authors also welcome other simple mobiles; the examples are not a set a family needs to acquire.

They place visual mobiles in the awake movement area, separate from the bed. Looking at the mobile from underneath helps an adult consider the baby’s view. They favor gentle movement from air currents and do not require accompanying music.

The authors watch for interest rather than a set viewing time. If the baby looks away, becomes tense or cries, they describe moving the mobile away, changing its position or trying another day. When reaching and batting begin, they distinguish sturdy tactile materials from these fragile looking mobiles.

entries.title: When looking becomes reaching
entries.summary: As a baby starts reaching and batting, the authors describe changing from fragile looking mobiles to sturdy tactile materials, with secure attachment and every part suitable for grasping and mouthing.
entries.cue: Your baby studies their hands, reaches toward a mobile or bats at it.
detail: A tactile mobile responds to the baby’s own movement. The book contrasts a bell that makes a sound when batted with a ring whose interest is in reaching, grasping and drawing it closer.
The authors require an attachment that withstands pulling, material suitable for the mouth and components that cannot come loose or become choking hazards.
As sitting develops, the book describes a different view: reaching forward rather than upward. Its discussion also cautions against propping a baby into sitting before they can get there themselves.

entries.title: An early grasp can be a reflex
entries.summary: The authors distinguish a newborn’s reflex grasp from the later choice to reach for an object. These are different moments in their account of hand movement.
entries.cue: Your baby’s fingers close around something touching their palm.
detail: In the first two months, the book describes fingers closing around an adult’s finger or an early grasping object. It later describes a baby studying their hands, reaching and batting with growing intention.

The authors distinguish this early grasp from independently using a rattle: recovering a dropped object also calls for movement such as turning or slithering. Their activity ages are guides, and they welcome seeking support for developmental concerns.

entries.title: A toy that stays put when touched
entries.summary: The appendix describes a toy on a suction base that rocks when batted but stays in place. The example depends on secure attachment and small parts remaining enclosed.
entries.cue: Your baby is interested in batting or reaching, while objects that move away are harder to return to.
detail: The toy’s fixed base offers a different experience from a rolling object: the baby can reach toward it again without the toy moving across the space. The authors’ example is a clear ball containing smaller balls, attached to a suction stand.

The row says “around 5+ months or once sitting.” The authors’ wider guidance favors activities that fit current interest and movement, and cautions against propping a baby into sitting before they can get there themselves.
